prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, changing how exporting, reallocation and the aggregate effects of trade are analysed

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B021 with Helpman and Melitz. The discovery is the selection model. Melitz (2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI moved trade analysis from industries to firms. They explain who exports, why liberalisation raises aggregate productivity through reallocation, and why trade has a within-industry channel that earlier models could not represent. The predictions have been confronted with firm-level data in many countries for more than twenty years, which is the combination of theory and credible micro evidence I weight most. The core work is mature, so timing is not an issue. The two-name attribution is among the cleanest on the shortlist, and Redding is a successor on quantitative and spatial extensions, not a co-originator. The distinction from Krugman (2008) is that this work concerns selection among heterogeneous firms, whereas that prize concerned increasing returns and variety at the industry level. I have changed the citation. Round 2 made me less comfortable with 'gains from trade' as its headline, so it now says 'aggregate effects of trade', which the selection mechanism supports more robustly. My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied entries, not on independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts that the model organised, and Eaton and Kortum offer a parallel structural route to quantitative gains from trade. None of them is on this entry, so a Helpman-Melitz prize could be read as rewarding the theory over the empirical groundwork. The welfare conclusions depend on functional-form assumptions such as Pareto productivity. As I recall, but have not verified, sufficient-statistics results suggest that the size of the gains from trade is less sensitive to the heterogeneity margin than the original framing implied. That weakens any citation built on gains from trade, and it is why I now centre the wording on selection and reallocation. Some members will also see the work as continuing the lineage recognised in 2008. Finally, B001 has broader opening support and larger policy reach, and its three-name core is more convergent. A reasonable member could weigh those facts more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B021 first. He treats Melitz (2003) as the central contribution and Helpman as completing the core, with Redding as derivative. He flags credit for Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and welfare sensitivity to Pareto assumptions. He also reports that I raised pairing Melitz with Eaton-Kortum-style quantitative work.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name core, and I share his view that Redding is a successor. One correction: my round 1 did not propose pairing Melitz with Eaton-Kortum. I listed them as credit concerns outside the entry. His conclusion is still right, because pairing would turn the discovery into quantitative gains from trade, a different and more contestable prize. On the chair's question, I do not think the omission of Bernard and Jensen makes the citation incomplete, provided it is worded around the selection model that organised their facts. It would be incomplete if it claimed credit for the empirical regularities themselves. I would add one caution to his Pareto discussion. That sensitivity is the reason I dropped 'gains from trade' as the citation's headline.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and B021 third. He argues that Melitz's contribution is largely one paper, that quantitative trade models may have partly absorbed it, that the omission of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum is a real weakness, and that it follows Krugman 2008 in the same field.
responses.response: I take the omission and the Krugman point seriously and have addressed both in the wording. On absorption, I read the quantitative models as nesting the heterogeneous-firm structure and not replacing it. Selection and reallocation remain the mechanisms inside them, and what is disputed is how much they matter for welfare. That is a limit on one use of the framework and does not undo the discovery. I also do not think one paper is a weakness when it reorganised a field. I accept that this puts more weight on Helpman's wider body of work than on Melitz alone, and I count that as part of the credit structure, not a flaw. I cannot rule out that the Committee sees a second step in the same lineage as too close to 2008. That is a real uncertainty for me.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B001 first and B021 third. He agrees B021 is strong and says he would support it if B001 stalls on attribution. He shares the credit concern about Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum and the Pareto sensitivity. He also notes that micro price evidence shows state dependence that Calvo pricing does not capture.
responses.response: I appreciate that he treats B021 as a genuine fallback, and it answers the chair's question on alternatives for me: I would accept B001 on the same basis. His micro-evidence point on pricing is the one that most affects my ranking between the two. It does not undermine the originating ideas, since a tractable benchmark need not be literally true. It does mean that the empirical standing of the Calvo device is weaker than its influence suggests. By contrast, the selection mechanism has been tested directly on firm-level data. That is a difference in the evidence behind the discovery, and it does not rest on how many members rank each part. I agree that the citation must be framed around selection to keep B021 coherent.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, separated by role. He asks whether the Taylor rule is a scientific contribution or a policy prescription, and he notes that attribution is broader than any trio. He ranks B021 fourth and treats Redding as a follower.
responses.response: His role-based separation is the strongest argument for B001, and it narrows the attribution gap I stressed in round 1. Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are separable in function in a way that Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are not. That is why I would support the trio if the Committee prefers it. Two things keep me at B021. First, his own open question on the Taylor rule shows that the B001 citation depends on a judgement about whether a rule is a discovery. B021 has no equivalent question. Second, the post-2021 and state-dependent-pricing evidence is mixed on the framework. I accept his view of Redding, which supports the two-name B021.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B002 first. He calls the Kiyotaki-Moore collateral mechanism foundational and tractable, with a clean two-author attribution. He acknowledges that the model is stylised, that identification of the collateral channel comes mostly from later work by others, and that the 2022 prize may reduce appetite for the theme.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution, and it is why B002 stays my second alternative. His candid statement about identification is the reason I do not rank it first. A mechanism can be influential and conceptually deep while its quantitative importance remains disputed, and the empirical support came mostly from later calibrated work. I would apply the same test to B021, where the firm-level tests are direct. The 2022 overlap is the weaker concern for me. The mechanism is distinct. If the Committee wants a macro-finance award, I would support the two-person Kiyotaki-Moore version without Gertler and Gilchrist. I would put B001 ahead of it as my first fallback.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats Helpman-Melitz as a distinct step from Krugman's 2008 prize or as the same lineage, and whether quantitative trade models are seen as having absorbed or merely extended the framework.
Whether a citation built on selection and reallocation can stand without Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, or whether their omission makes the award look incomplete.
How robust the aggregate-welfare implications are to Pareto and other functional-form assumptions, and whether that should shape the citation wording.

Whether B001's convergent three-name core and broader policy reach should outweigh the mixed empirical record of its framework. If the Committee prefers B001, I would support Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, with a citation centred on the originating ideas.
My assessments rely on general knowledge and the supplied files, not on independent verification of the literature or of priority claims.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Helpman or Melitz, or for the credited names in B001 and B002. I am an empirical labour economist at Uppsala. My profile records no co-authorship with any shortlisted candidate. Disclosures, none adjudicated: I was a professor at Stockholm University from 2010 to 2017 and overlapped institutionally with the IIES macro group, with no co-authorship with Persson or other B006 candidates. Other members report an IIES proximity between Krusell and Persson, and I take no position on it. My field is close to B010, B014 and B047, none of which is in my configuration. Bertil Holmlund is my long-standing co-author, and another member's file lists him among her frequent co-authors. He is not a candidate.
